titel: Sharp knives: cutting instead of crushing
kurz: A sharp blade cuts cells cleanly, a blunt one crushes them. You notice it in watering eyes over onions, brown edges on herbs and juice on the board.
bild_im_kopf: Like scissors and pliers: both separate things, but only one leaves clean edges.
was_passiert: Cutting with a blunt knife needs pressure, and the pressure tears many cells beside the cut. Their contents leak out: in [[zwiebel|onions]] this produces the irritant, in herbs the cut edge browns. A 2025 study showed that blunt blades spray more fine droplets from the onion. Over time the fine edge bends over. A honing steel straightens it again; only a whetstone removes metal and forms a new edge.
warum_wichtig: A sharp knife is safer because it doesn't slip, and it makes cut food look better and keep longer.
faustregeln: For onions: a sharp knife, because fewer damaged cells release less irritant.
For herbs: slice through in one cut rather than chopping, because crushed leaves turn black.
Keep it out of the dishwasher: heat, detergent and knocks dull the edge.
schritte: Before cooking, draw the blade over the honing steel a few times on each side, at a shallow angle.
If the knife no longer slices through a tomato skin, it needs sharpening.
On a whetstone, sharpen at a constant angle of about 15 to 20 degrees, coarse first, then fine.
Cut with a drawing motion instead of just pressing down.
Cut on wood or plastic, not on glass or stone.
